additions.title: Investigation: WannaCry cyber attack and the NHS
additions.locator: Summary, paragraphs 9 and 10; Part Three, paragraph 3.3. HC 414, Session 2017-2019
additions.quote: had not tested the plan at a local level. This meant the NHS was not clear what actions it should take when affected by WannaCry
additions.why: Official audit finding on what an unrehearsed plan is worth: a response plan existed but had never been exercised locally, so it was unclear who should lead and communications failed. The cover is dated 25 April 2018; the report is signed 24 October 2017. A cyber attack on the NHS in 2017, not an AI failure.

additions.title: Capita fined £14m for data breach affecting over 6m people
additions.locator: Sections 'The cyber attack' and 'Summary of the contraventions'
additions.quote: Capita took 58 hours to respond appropriately, against a target response time of one hour.
additions.why: Enforcement decision that turns on detection-to-response time: an alert was raised within ten minutes but the device was not quarantined for 58 hours; the security operations centre was understaffed. The regulator's statement was read, not the full penalty notice. Settled by agreement; a cyber attack, not an AI system.

additions.title: The Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018, regulation 11: The duty to notify incidents
additions.quote: without undue delay and in any event no later than 72 hours after the operator is aware that a NIS incident has occurred
additions.why: A second binding reporting window to map beforehand, separate from the data protection one: operators of essential services must notify their competent authority of an incident with a significant impact on continuity of the service. Applies only to designated operators of essential services (regulation 12 covers digital service providers). The page showed no known outstanding effects; a Bill to reform these Regulations was before Parliament and no Act was found on legislation.gov.uk on the date checked.

additions.title: Towards a common reporting framework for AI incidents
additions.locator: Abstract and Executive summary; OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 34
additions.quote: learn from AI harms identified elsewhere in the world
additions.why: International comparator. Sets out 29 criteria for describing an AI incident so that reports can be compared across countries; useful as a template for what an internal AI incident record should capture. A policy paper, not a binding instrument; it creates no duty to report.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
additions.locator: Table 4 (MANAGE function), MANAGE 4.3; also MANAGE 4.1 and, in Table 1, GOVERN 4.3
additions.quote: Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities.
additions.why: The AI-specific standard for the response and learning loop: incidents and errors are tracked, responded to, recovered from and documented, and the people affected are told. Voluntary; a United States framework.

additions.title: Preventing Repeated Real World AI Failures by Cataloging Incidents: The AI Incident Database
additions.quote: Intelligent systems currently cause real world harms without a collective memory of their failings.
additions.why: The research case for the learning loop: without incident records, organisations repeat the same failures. Describes a public database of more than 1,000 incident reports. Preprint of a paper accepted to the Innovative Applications of Artificial Intelligence conference (IAAI-21); descriptive, not an evaluation of any response process.

additions.title: Lessons for Editors of AI Incidents from the AI Incident Database
additions.publisher: arXiv (Paeth, Atherton, Pittaras, Frase and McGregor)
additions.quote: epistemic uncertainty in AI incident reporting is unavoidable
additions.why: Reviews more than 750 recorded AI incidents and finds that cause, extent of harm and severity are often unclear when an incident is logged. Supports writing incident processes that work with incomplete facts. Preprint, not peer reviewed in the version read; based on publicly reported incidents only.

additions.title: AI incident reporting: Addressing a gap in the UK's regulation of AI
additions.locator: Summary page, section 'The need for incident reporting'
additions.quote: the UK’s regulation of AI currently lacks an effective incident reporting framework
additions.why: A UK policy institute's analysis, consistent with the brief's statement that no UK law sets a general duty to report AI failures. Recommends that government report incidents in its own use of AI. A think-tank report, not peer reviewed and not official; only the summary page was read.

rejected.title: ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO 22301 (standard-setter's own pages)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to automated reading, as in the first pass. Not bypassed; no ISO claim made.

rejected.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), EUR-Lex
rejected.reason: HTTP 202 with an empty body. Not read; no DORA claim made.

rejected.title: Computer Security Incident Response Recommendations (NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3)
rejected.reason: Opened (April 2025). General cyber incident response; the AI RMF speaks to AI incidents directly, so adding it would be padding.

rejected.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI (Singapore)
rejected.reason: HTTP 404 at the address tried; not read.

rejected.title: Parliament Bill page, Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 with a browser check. Not bypassed.

brief_check: One point is dated. The Commission's AI Act Service Desk page for Article 73 now shows the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026 with no 'not yet updated' notice and no AMENDED marker on that article, so the brief's 'that text is being amended' and the reading-list note on Article 73 should be re-read; paragraph 2 still shows 15 days. Nothing else read contradicts the brief.
